claim: Zebrafish primordial germ cells (PGCs) migrate as single cells within a complex environment from the position where they are specified towards their target.
source: As a useful in vivo model for exploring the regulation and function of filopodia in cell migration, we employed zebrafish Primordial germ cells (PGCs). These cells perform long-range migration as single cells within a complex environment from the position where they are specified towards their target (Richardson and Lehmann, 2010; Tarbashevich and Raz, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Richardson and Lehmann, 2010 and Tarbashevich and Raz, 2010.

claim: PGC migration is guided by the chemokine Cxcl12a that binds Cxcr4b, which is expressed on the surface of these cells.
source: PGC migration is guided by the chemokine Cxcl12a that binds Cxcr4b, which is expressed on the surface of these cells (Doitsidou et al., 2002; Knaut et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Doitsidou et al., 2002 and Knaut et al., 2003.

claim: The Cxcr4b-Cxcl12a receptor-ligand pair controls stem-cell homing, cancer metastasis, and inflammation.
source: This specific receptor-ligand pair has been shown to control among other processes, stem-cell homing (Chute, 2006), cancer metastasis (Zlotnik, 2008) and inflammation (Werner et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chute, 2006; Zlotnik, 2008; and Werner et al., 2013.

claim: The level of GFP-tagged Cxcr4b measured at the cell front and its back was similar in migrating PGCs.
source: Similar to findings in Dictyostelium discoideum cells, in which the guidance receptor is evenly distributed around the cell membrane (Ueda et al., 2001) and consistent with our previous results (Minina et al., 2007), the level of a GFP-tagged Cxcr4b (expressed at low amounts that do not affect the migration) measured at the cell front and its back was similar (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citations to Ueda et al., 2001 and Minina et al., 2007.

claim: The receptor turnover on the plasma membrane did not reveal a significant difference between the front and the back of the cell.
source: Furthermore, the receptor turnover on the plasma membrane, as visualized by a Cxcr4b tandem fluorescent timer (tft) (Khmelinskii et al., 2012) expressed in PGCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), which are directed by the endogenous Cxcl12a gradient (Figure 1B), did not reveal a significant difference between the front and the back of the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E, and a citation to Khmelinskii et al., 2012.

claim: Zebrafish PGCs generate blebs primarily at the cell aspect facing the migration direction.
source: Guided towards their target by the chemokine Cxcl12a, zebrafish PGCs generate blebs primarily at the cell aspect facing the migration direction (Reichman-Fried et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reichman-Fried et al., 2004.

claim: F-actin was detected in all of the filopodia formed at the cell front.
source: While F-actin was detected in all of the filopodia formed at the cell front, about 50% of those localized to the back of the cell showed no detectable actin signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), pointing at differences in actin content between the two populations of filopodia.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: About 50% of filopodia localized to the back of the cell showed no detectable actin signal.
source: While F-actin was detected in all of the filopodia formed at the cell front, about 50% of those localized to the back of the cell showed no detectable actin signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), pointing at differences in actin content between the two populations of filopodia.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Migrating PGCs show on average 5.6 ± 0.5 filopodia at any given time point.
source: We found that at any given time point, migrating PGCs show on average 5.6 ± 0.5 filopodia, with a strong bias for filopodia generation at the cell front (wild type in Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Migrating PGCs show a strong bias for filopodia generation at the cell front.
source: We found that at any given time point, migrating PGCs show on average 5.6 ± 0.5 filopodia, with a strong bias for filopodia generation at the cell front (wild type in Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Blebs can form in parts of the cells where filopodia are not present.
source: Specifically, we found that blebs can form in parts of the cells where filopodia are not present (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B, red asterisk in 40″, Video 2) and conversely, filopodia were maintained close to a forming bleb (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, arrowheads in 20″, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B and Video 2.

claim: Filopodia were maintained close to a forming bleb.
source: Specifically, we found that blebs can form in parts of the cells where filopodia are not present (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B, red asterisk in 40″, Video 2) and conversely, filopodia were maintained close to a forming bleb (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, arrowheads in 20″, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and Video 2.

claim: Filopodia in the front persisted for 28 ± 3.5 s and were 3.0 ± 0.1 µm long.
source: That is, while filopodia in the front persisted for 28 ± 3.5 s and were 3.0 ± 0.1 µm long, filopodia at the back of the cell persisted for 51 ± 8.2 s and were 4.3 ± 0.4 µm long (wild type in Figure 3A,B), thus revealing that filopodia located at the cell front are significantly more dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Filopodia at the back of the cell persisted for 51 ± 8.2 s and were 4.3 ± 0.4 µm long.
source: That is, while filopodia in the front persisted for 28 ± 3.5 s and were 3.0 ± 0.1 µm long, filopodia at the back of the cell persisted for 51 ± 8.2 s and were 4.3 ± 0.4 µm long (wild type in Figure 3A,B), thus revealing that filopodia located at the cell front are significantly more dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Filopodia located at the cell front are significantly more dynamic than those at the back.
source: That is, while filopodia in the front persisted for 28 ± 3.5 s and were 3.0 ± 0.1 µm long, filopodia at the back of the cell persisted for 51 ± 8.2 s and were 4.3 ± 0.4 µm long (wild type in Figure 3A,B), thus revealing that filopodia located at the cell front are significantly more dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Only 30% of the filopodia at the cell front were engulfed by forming blebs.
source: Only 30% of the filopodia at the cell front were engulfed by forming blebs and those that were not engulfed showed a reduced persistence as compared with filopodia formed at the cell back (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Filopodia at the cell front that were not engulfed by blebs showed a reduced persistence as compared with filopodia formed at the cell back.
source: Only 30% of the filopodia at the cell front were engulfed by forming blebs and those that were not engulfed showed a reduced persistence as compared with filopodia formed at the cell back (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PGCs in medNY054 embryos show a dramatic increase in the number of filopodia (11.4 ± 0.8) relative to wild type (5.6 ± 0.5).
source: PGCs in medNY054 embryos show a dramatic increase in the number of filopodia (11.4 ± 0.8, Figure 2C, whole cell) relative to wild type (5.6 ± 0.5, Figure 2C, whole cell).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PGCs in medNY054 embryos show an even distribution of filopodia around the cell circumference.
source: PGCs in medNY054 embryos also show an even distribution of filopodia around the cell circumference, which is in sharp contrast to the polar distribution observed in the wild type embryos (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Filopodia of PGCs in medNY054 embryos revealed average persistence (51 ± 3.1 s) and maximum lengths (3.9 ± 0.1 µm) similar to filopodia located at the back of wild type PGCs.
source: Strikingly, irrespective of their position around the cell perimeter, filopodia of PGCs in medNY054 embryos revealed average persistence (51 ± 3.1 s, Figure 3A, whole cell) and maximum lengths (3.9 ± 0.1 µm Figure 3B, whole cell) similar to filopodia located at the back of wild type PGCs (Figure 3A,B, wild type).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The graded distribution of Cxcl12 determines the number, the distribution and the dynamic behaviour of filopodia around the PGC circumference.
source: We conclude therefore, that the graded distribution of Cxcl12 determines the number, the distribution and the dynamic behaviour of filopodia around the PGC circumference.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing differences in filopodia properties in wild type versus medNY054 embryos and under uniform Cxcl12a conditions.

claim: PGCs respond to the Cxcl12a gradient first by formation of filopodia oriented towards the Cxcl12a source and then by cell polarization and migration in the direction of the chemokine.
source: These experiments show that PGCs respond to the Cxcl12a gradient first by formation of filopodia oriented towards the Cxcl12a source and then by cell polarization and migration in the direction of the chemokine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the transplantation experiments described in the text and shown in Figure 4 and Video 6.

claim: Cxcl12a-Venus foci that were initially detected on the cell surface were subsequently internalized into the cell.
source: As shown in Figure 5B and Video 8, Cxcl12a-Venus foci that were initially detected on the cell surface were subsequently internalized into the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Video 8.

claim: A similar interaction between Cxcl12 foci and PGCs was observed on the surface of filopodia.
source: Strikingly, a similar interaction between Cxcl12 foci and PGCs was observed on the surface of filopodia (Figure 5C and Video 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Video 9.

claim: Binding of Cxcl12 was observed at the tip of a filopodium that extended about 12 µm away from the cell body.
source: Binding of Cxcl12 was observed at the tip of a filopodium (red arrowhead in Figure 5C) that extended about 12 µm away from the cell body, as well as closer to the cell body (yellow arrowhead in Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Retraction of the filopodium resulted in dragging of the distant Cxcl12 focus to the cell body.
source: Retraction of the filopodium resulted in dragging of the distant Cxcl12 focus to the cell body and a bleb forming at this location engulfs the closer Cxcl12 focus (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The irsp53 RNA is maternally provided and ubiquitously present in 1-hr post fertilization (hpf) embryos, as well as at later stages (6 and 10 hpf).
source: Specifically, irsp53 RNA is maternally provided and ubiquitously present in 1-hr post fertilization (hpf) embryos, as well as at later stages (6 and 10 hpf, Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: An Irsp53-mCherry fusion protein was expressed in the cytoplasm and importantly, in filopodia, particularly in those located at the cell front.
source: We also found that an Irsp53-mCherry fusion protein (Figure 6A) was expressed in the cytoplasm and importantly, in filopodia (Figure 6C, upper panel and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), particularly in those located at the cell front.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of the DN Irsp53 version in PGCs resulted in a significant decrease in filopodia number at the cell front.
source: Moreover, expression of the DN Irsp53 version in PGCs resulted in a significant decrease in filopodia number at the cell front (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Inhibition of Irsp53 function had no effect on filopodia formation in medNY054 embryos.
source: However, inhibition of Irsp53 function had no effect on filopodia formation in medNY054 embryos (Figure 6F,G), in which the filopodia exhibit posterior characteristics (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Inhibition of Irsp53 function had no effect on the formation of blebs at the PGC front in embryos lacking the guidance cue.
source: The inhibition of Irsp53 function specifically affected filopodia formation rather than influencing cell migration in general, as this treatment had no effect on the formation of blebs at the PGC front in embryos lacking the guidance cue (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Irsp53 is required for filopodia formation in response to Cxcl12a gradient.
source: These results provide evidence that Irsp53 is required for filopodia formation in response to Cxcl12a gradient and can serve as a specific reagent for interfering with their formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that DN Irsp53 reduces filopodia at the cell front in wild type but not in medNY054 embryos.

claim: When an mCherry-tagged version of Afap1L1a was expressed in PGCs, it was found to be specifically enriched at the base of most filopodia (84 ± 9.7%) at the level of the cell cortex.
source: Namely, when an mCherry-tagged version of Afap1L1a (Figure 7A) was expressed in PGCs, it was found to be specifically enriched at the base of most filopodia (84 ± 9.7%) at the level of the cell cortex (Figure 7C), suggesting a function for the protein in filopodia formation or maintenance.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: afap1l1a RNA is maternally provided and is uniformly expressed during early embryonic development.
source: We subsequently ascertained that afap1l1a RNA is expressed at the time at which PGCs migrate towards their target and showed that afap1l1a RNA is maternally provided and is uniformly expressed during early embryonic development (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Overexpression of Afap1L1a resulted in a significant increase in filopodia number as compared to control cells.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of the protein resulted in a significant increase in filopodia number as compared to control cells (Figure 7D, whole cell).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Overexpression of Afap1L1a changed the distribution of the filopodia significantly, resulting in a decrease in filopodia number at the cell front and an increase in number at the sides and back of the cells.
source: Furthermore, this treatment changed the distribution of the filopodia significantly, resulting in a decrease in filopodia number at the cell front and an increase in number at the sides and back of the cells (Figure 7D,E), effectively reversing the normal distribution of filopodia in the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Overexpression of Afap1L1a did not significantly alter bleb formation at the PGC front in embryos lacking the guidance cue.
source: Similar to the Irsp53 effect, overexpression of Afap1L1a did not significantly alter bleb formation at the PGC front in embryos lacking the guidance cue (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In response to a graded Cxcl12a concentration in the environment, zebrafish PGCs exhibit increased pH at the cell front (7% higher on the logarithmic pH scale, reflecting difference of 15% at the level of H+ concentration).
source: To this end, we made use of our recent findings showing that in response to a graded Cxcl12a concentration in the environment, zebrafish PGCs exhibit increased pH at the cell front (7% higher on the logarithmic pH scale, reflecting difference of 15% at the level of H+ concentration).
evidence: The claim is based on recent findings by the authors, as indicated by the reference to their work.

claim: The polar pH elevation could control the activity of various proteins important for cell motility and in the case of PGCs, was shown to be essential for a local increase in the activity of the small GTPase Rac1 and thus, for directing actin polymerization to the cell front.
source: This polar pH elevation could control the activity of various proteins important for cell motility (Stock and Schwab, 2009) and in the case of PGCs, was shown to be essential for a local increase in the activity of the small GTPase Rac1 and thus, for directing actin polymerization to the cell front (Tarbashevich et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stock and Schwab, 2009 and Tarbashevich et al., 2015.

claim: The loss of the Cxcl12a gradient leads to the loss of the difference in pH between the cell front and its rear.
source: The loss of the Cxcl12a gradient leads the loss of the difference in pH between the cell front and its rear (Tarbashevich et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tarbashevich et al., 2015.

claim: The reduction of filopodia formation at the cell front reduced (in the case of Irsp53), or abolished (in the case of the Afap1L1a) the increased pH at the leading edge.
source: Strikingly, the reduction of filopodia formation at the cell front reduced (in the case of Irsp53), or abolished (in the case of the Afap1L1a) the increased pH at the leading edge (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Inhibiting the relative elevation of pH at the cell front by inhibiting the translation of the Carbonic anhydrase 15b had no effect on filopodia formation.
source: Conversely, inhibiting the relative elevation of pH at the cell front by inhibiting the translation of the Carbonic anhydrase 15b (Tarbashevich et al., 2015) had no effect on filopodia formation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation to Tarbashevich et al., 2015.

claim: Rac1 activity was significantly reduced in cells overexpressing Afap1L1a as compared with control cells.
source: Importantly, as compared with control cells, Rac1 activity was significantly reduced in these cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of a constitutively activated version of Rac1 (Rac1V12) in germ cells had no effect on filopodia formation beyond the increase in their numbers observed in cells rendered immotile.
source: Consistent with the idea that filopodia function upstream of the Cxcl12a signalling cascade, expression of a constitutively activated version of Rac1 (Rac1V12) in germ cells (that stop migrating as a result) had no effect on filopodia formation beyond the increase in their numbers observed in cells rendered immotile (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: When filopodia function at the cell front is hindered, the ability of the PGCs to effectively sense the chemokine gradient is impaired, as reflected by the lack of elevated pH and by the reduced Rac1 activity at the leading edge.
source: These results suggest that when filopodia function at the cell front is hindered, the ability of the PGCs to effectively sense the chemokine gradient is impaired, as reflected by the lack of elevated pH and by the reduced Rac1 activity at the leading edge.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that manipulating filopodia affects pH and Rac1 activity.

claim: Filopodia function in controlling intracellular pH at the cell front and are formed independent of it.
source: These results are also consistent with the idea that as a cellular structure, filopodia function in controlling intracellular pH at the cell front and are formed independent of it.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that inhibiting pH elevation does not affect filopodia formation, but inhibiting filopodia affects pH.

claim: PGCs expressing the DN Irsp53 protein exhibited a significant reduction in displacement as a result of reduced track straightness.
source: Interestingly, PGCs expressing the DN Irsp53 protein exhibited a significant reduction in displacement (the shortest distance between the start and end points) as a result of reduced track straightness (the degree of changes in path direction) (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Inhibition of Irsp53 function in medNY054 embryos lacking functional chemokine had no effect on the migration tracks of PGCs.
source: The specific role of front filopodia in the response to the chemokine gradient is further highlighted by the finding, that inhibition of Irsp53 function in medNY054 embryos lacking functional chemokine had no effect on the migration tracks of PGCs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Irsp53, which specifically affects filopodia formation at the cell front, is not essential for the migratory behaviour per se, but is rather important in the context of chemotaxis.
source: These results also emphasize the fact that Irsp53, which specifically affects filopodia formation at the cell front, is not essential for the migratory behaviour per se, but is rather important in the context of chemotaxis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that DN Irsp53 affects migration in wild type but not in medNY054 embryos.

claim: Overexpression of the Afap1L1a in PGCs led to a reduction in cell displacement, track straightness and speed.
source: Alterations in the migration track properties were observed yet to a greater extent, upon overexpression of the Afap1L1a in PGCs. Specifically, overexpression of the Afap1L1a that led to a reversal of filopodia distribution with predominance of filopodia in the back, also led to a reduction in cell displacement, track straightness and speed (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: Tight regulation of filopodia formation and distribution around the cell surface is essential for effective guided PGC migration.
source: We conclude therefore, that tight regulation of filopodia formation and distribution around the cell surface is essential for effective guided PGC migration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that manipulating filopodia affects migration characteristics.

claim: The defects in the dynamic characteristics of cell migration manifested in the cell tracks of manipulated PGCs resulted in an increased proportion of chemokine-guided cells that failed to reach their target at 24 hpf.
source: The defects in the dynamic characteristics of cell migration manifested in the cell tracks of manipulated PGCs resulted in an increased proportion of chemokine-guided cells that failed to reach their target at 24 hpf (Figure 9E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9E–H.

claim: Filopodia are asymmetrically formed in response to a chemokine gradient and in turn, play a critical role in polarization of cells and their response to directional cues.
source: In this work we provide evidence that filopodia are asymmetrically formed in response to a chemokine gradient and in turn, play a critical role in polarization of cells and their response to directional cues.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Filopodia properties differ in the front from the back of the cell, such that front filopodia are larger in number, turn over more rapidly, are shorter and contain more F-actin.
source: We found that filopodia properties differ in the front from the back of the cell, such that front filopodia are larger in number, turn over more rapidly, are shorter and contain more F-actin.
evidence: The claim is based on data presented in Figures 2 and 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: These differences in filopodia distribution and dynamics are governed by the graded distribution of the chemokine in the environment.
source: These differences in filopodia distribution and dynamics are governed by the graded distribution of the chemokine in the environment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that filopodia properties change in the absence of Cxcl12a gradient.

claim: The chemokine appears to bind and be transported on the filopodium, followed by internalization.
source: Our finding that the chemokine appears to bind and be transported on the filopodium, followed by internalization, is consistent with the idea that filopodia function in Cxcl12a uptake and in increasing the surface relevant for this action at the cell front.
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 8 and 9.

claim: Filopodia function in Cxcl12a uptake and in increasing the surface relevant for this action at the cell front.
source: Our finding that the chemokine appears to bind and be transported on the filopodium, followed by internalization, is consistent with the idea that filopodia function in Cxcl12a uptake and in increasing the surface relevant for this action at the cell front.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of Cxcl12a binding and internalization on filopodia.

claim: Specifically decreasing filopodia formation at the cell front (by inhibiting Irsp53 function) resulted in inefficient propagation of the external signal into the cell as evidenced by the strong reduction in the difference between the pH at the cell front and its back.
source: The effect of specifically decreasing filopodia formation at the cell front (by inhibiting Irsp53 function) resulted in inefficient propagation of the external signal into the cell as evidenced by the strong reduction in the difference between the pH at the cell front and its back.
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Overexpression of the Afap1L1 protein erased the normal front-back polarity with respect to filopodia distribution.
source: In the same direction, overexpression of the Afap1L1 protein erased the normal front-back polarity with respect to filopodia distribution.
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: In the absence of polar distribution of filopodia in the direction of the attractive cue, the cells could not effectively detect the graded chemokine cue, establish a stable front and thus, did not elevate the pH and Rac1 activity at the leading edge.
source: In the absence of polar distribution of filopodia in the direction of the attractive cue, the cells could not effectively detect the graded chemokine cue, establish a stable front and thus, did not elevate the pH and Rac1 activity at the leading edge.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that manipulating filopodia distribution affects pH and Rac1 activity.

claim: These effects on the characteristic front-back cell polarity impaired the directional migration in response to a guidance cue, culminating in ectopic localization of the cells at the end of the migration process.
source: These effects on the characteristic front-back cell polarity impaired the directional migration in response to a guidance cue, culminating in ectopic localization of the cells at the end of the migration process.
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Following the activation of Cxcr4b by Cxcl12a, the scaffold protein Irsp53 is activated to promote the formation of dynamic filopodia at the cell front.
source: We suggest that following the activation of Cxcr4b by Cxcl12a, the scaffold protein Irsp53 is activated to promote the formation of dynamic filopodia at the cell front.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and represents a proposed model.

claim: These filopodia extend in the direction of higher chemokine concentration and expand the surface for Cxcl12a binding, thereby further enhancing Cxcr4b signalling at the cell front and effectively enhancing the absolute differences in ligand levels detected along the front-back axis of the cell.
source: These filopodia extend in the direction of higher chemokine concentration and expand the surface for Cxcl12a binding, thereby further enhancing Cxcr4b signalling at the cell front and effectively enhancing the absolute differences in ligand levels detected along the front-back axis of the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and represents a proposed model.

claim: The positive feedback loop allows the PGCs to interpret shallow gradients by forming a front that is more sensitive to the guidance cue.
source: We suggest that the positive feedback loop presented in Figure 10 allows the PGCs to interpret shallow gradients by forming a front that is more sensitive to the guidance cue.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and represents a proposed model shown in Figure 10.

claim: The uneven receptor activation along the back–front axis of the cell that includes the filopodia is a prerequisite for the establishment of the intracellular elevated pH at the cell front that facilitates actin polymerization at this location leading to functional polarization of the cell.
source: The uneven receptor activation along the back–front axis of the cell that includes the filopodia is a prerequisite for the establishment of the intracellular elevated pH at the cell front that facilitates actin polymerization at this location (Tarbashevich et al., 2015) leading to functional polarization of the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and a citation to Tarbashevich et al., 2015.

claim: Under conditions of no, or uniform activation of Cxcr4b a cell front is not established.
source: Under conditions of no, or uniform activation of Cxcr4b a cell front is not established.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that cells in medNY054 embryos or under uniform Cxcl12a do not show polarized filopodia or pH.

claim: In such cases, the positive feedback loop that normally stabilizes the front in one aspect of the migrating cell is not present, affecting cell polarity and the features of migration in the direction of the chemokine source.
source: In such cases, the positive feedback loop that normally stabilizes the front in one aspect of the migrating cell is not present, affecting cell polarity and the features of migration in the direction of the chemokine source.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and represents a proposed model.

claim: CDC42 was shown to be active at the leading edge of migrating cells and in neuronal growth cones.
source: CDC42 was shown to be active at the leading edge of migrating cells and in neuronal growth cones (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002; Nalbant et al., 2004), and IRSp53 was shown to be one of the effectors of CDC42 (Govind et al., 2001; Krugmann et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002 and Nalbant et al., 2004.

claim: IRSp53 was shown to be one of the effectors of CDC42.
source: CDC42 was shown to be active at the leading edge of migrating cells and in neuronal growth cones (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002; Nalbant et al., 2004), and IRSp53 was shown to be one of the effectors of CDC42 (Govind et al., 2001; Krugmann et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Govind et al., 2001 and Krugmann et al., 2001.

claim: Tracheal cells were shown to generate morphologically different populations of cytonemes, each responding specifically to different secreted signals.
source: The finding that at least two populations of filopodia formed on the surface of migrating PGCs and that these populations exhibit differences concerning their distribution and dynamic properties are reminiscent of the findings concerning cytonemes in Drosophila (Roy et al., 2011). In this case, tracheal cells were shown to generate morphologically different populations of cytonemes, each responding specifically to different secreted signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roy et al., 2011.

claim: Some filopodia adhere to somatic cells, appear to be under tension and can pull particles towards the cell.
source: This possibility is supported by the observations that some filopodia adhere to somatic cells, appear to be under tension and can pull particles towards the cell (Kress et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kress et al., 2007.

claim: Upon laser-mediated cutting of a filopodium, its distal tip remained attached to a cell in the environment, while the proximal part attached to the cell rapidly retracted.
source: Upon laser-mediated cutting of a filopodium of this kind, its distal tip remained attached to a cell in the environment, while the proximal part attached to the cell rapidly retracted (see Video 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Video 10.

claim: The function of filopodia in decoding the Cxcl12a gradient in the context of PGC migration must bear on cancer cell invasion, since Cxcl12 is known to play a key role in metastasis of several cancer types.
